name: r2-external-2
statement: The cued base's two temperature failure modes come from one global temperature acting on two kinds of positions: at its rare high-entropy fork tokens the progress continuations split their mass while one restatement of an earlier step keeps its own, so T 0.6 or top-p 0.95 hands the fork to the restatement and starts a self-reinforcing loop, while at its many near-deterministic tokens T 1.0 samples tail tokens that become slips; RL sharpens the fork tokens onto one progress continuation and lowers entropy elsewhere, which is why it is temperature-insensitive, and a per-position temperature (1.0 at forks, 0.6 elsewhere) gives the base the loop-free finishing of T 1.0 and the finished-answer accuracy of T 0.6.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base with and without the opening cue, and Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math, MATH-500 and the 328 harder problems, cap 16,384, sampling at T 0.6-1.0 and top-p 0.95-1.0, including per-position temperature schedules gated on the model's own next-token entropy. Does not cover non-loop drift to the cap, wrong methods, the weight-difference studies, or the 'Answer:' format change.

explains.how: At T 0.6 with top-p 0.95 both the low temperature and the cut tail push fork tokens toward the restatement, so loops take a quarter of the answers.
Restoring the tail at forks gives back the low-probability progress continuations, so cap hits fall from 119 to 98 at the same temperature.
With cap hits counted wrong, T 0.6 gets 378 of 402 finished answers right (94.0 %): at T 0.6 the base's finished answers are accurate; its failure is loops.
At T 1.0 the base finishes 473 answers but gets 410 right (86.7 %): the loops are gone and the finished-answer accuracy drops by 7 points, the tail-sampling cost at near-deterministic tokens.

explains.quote: Plain base: T 1.0 - T 0.6 = -28.0, -29.6, -27.2, 0.0 by quartile
explains.how: Short solutions have few forks, so raising T only adds tail-sampled slips; on the longest solutions it also removes loops, and the two effects cancel.
Short base answers at T 1.0 are wrong where RL's are not; short answers have no loop to explain them, so a per-token slip mechanism is left.
Slips are a named share of the RL-only items at T 1.0, the error kind tail sampling at near-deterministic tokens produces.
RL's forks no longer hold a near-tie with a restatement and its other tokens are sharper, so neither failure mode depends on T.
RL's largest changes on the base's cap-hit problems are at discourse fork tokens, the positions where the theory places the loop-starting choice.
RL changes the top choice at a small minority of positions, the size of the base's high-entropy fork set.

explains.quote: base entropy finds those positions with AUROC 0.94-0.98
explains.how: The positions RL changes are found by the base's own entropy, so a gate on base entropy picks the same positions without RL.

explains.quote: the base's loops have periods of hundreds of characters
explains.how: The loops repeat whole reasoning steps, as expected when a fork chooses to restate an earlier step rather than when tokens stutter.

conflicts.how: At T 1.0 a quarter of RL-only items are long non-repeating runs to the cap, which neither fork restatement nor tail slips explains.

conflicts.quote: from RL's prefix 48 / 41 / 21; from its own prefix 23 / 16 / 38
conflicts.how: At one fixed temperature the base finishes twice as often from RL's prefix as from its own: part of the loop risk lives in the context, not in the sampler.

conflicts.quote: Fixed rules: forced 'Wait', logit bias, greedy first 100 tokens, entropy stop
conflicts.how: Published entropy-based and fixed decoding rules score at or below the base on other models, so a sampler-only gain of 15 items is against the published trend.

conflicts.quote: power sampling / MCMC: +2.4 to +3.5 points on MATH-500
conflicts.how: The best published sampling method recovers only 2-3.5 points, less than this theory predicts for a per-position temperature.
RL at T 1.0 also samples its own near-deterministic tokens at full temperature yet loses nothing; the theory needs RL's non-fork tokens to be much sharper than the base's, which no item measures.

rival: The remaining gap is set by the weights (self-conditioning on long context, verification, or a stop policy), and the sampler only trades loops for slips along one curve whose best point is T 1.0. It predicts any per-position schedule mixing T 0.6 and T 1.0 lands between 378 and 410 on the cued base, and that the inverted schedule (T 0.6 at forks) and the gated one do about the same. This theory predicts the gated schedule beats T 1.0 (about 425) and the inverted schedule loops like T 0.6 (about 95 cap hits).

predictions.experiment: Base + cue, per-position temperature: T 1.0 where the model's own next-token entropy (computed at T 1) exceeds 0.672 nats, T 0.6 elsewhere; top-p 1.0, MATH-500 n=500, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample: right
predictions.refuted_by: 410 or fewer right (no better than plain T 1.0)

predictions.experiment: Same run: rule-A loops (zlib rule of knowledge-787e53)
predictions.refuted_by: 25 or more rule-A loops (loops also start at low-entropy positions)

predictions.experiment: Base + cue, inverted schedule: T 0.6 where the model's own next-token entropy exceeds 0.672 nats, T 1.0 elsewhere; top-p 1.0, MATH-500 n=500, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample: cap hits
predictions.refuted_by: 50 or fewer cap hits (low temperature at forks does not start loops)

predictions.experiment: Plain base (no cue), the gated schedule of the first prediction (T 1.0 above 0.672 nats, T 0.6 elsewhere), top-p 1.0, MATH-500 n=500, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample: right (plain base: 305-319 at T 0.6, 224 at T 1.0)
predictions.refuted_by: 319 or fewer right (no better than the plain base's best global temperature)

predictions.experiment: Saved base + cue answers at T 0.6 / top-p 1.0 (result-dadeec cell) with a rule-A loop: teacher-forced base entropy at the position that emits the first token of the first repeated block; fraction of loops where that entropy is above the answer's own 80th entropy percentile
predictions.refuted_by: 0.35 or less (loop onsets are not at high-entropy fork positions; base rate is 0.2)

predictions.experiment: Base + cue, the gated schedule of the first prediction, the 328 harder problems, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample: right (base + cue at T 1.0: 164)

imports.finding: Loops come from risk aversion: when the progress-making action is hard to learn its mass is spread across alternatives while an easy cyclic action keeps its mass, so low temperature selects the cyclic action; temperature removes loops but not the underlying error.
imports.how: Locates the loop-starting choice at specific positions (forks where progress mass is split) rather than everywhere, which is what makes a per-position temperature predict anything different from a global one.

imports.finding: Only about 20 % of chain-of-thought tokens have entropy above 0.672 nats; RLVR keeps the base's high-entropy positions and changes the policy mainly there.
imports.how: Identifies the forks of 2512.12895 with the base's own high-entropy minority, gives the threshold for the gate, and explains why RL, which sharpens exactly those positions, stops looping at low temperature; the combination predicts the gated schedule beats both global temperatures and the inverted one loops.

imports.finding: Small temperature or top-p gives the boredom trap (repetition); large gives the confusion trap (incoherent errors).
imports.how: Assigns the two traps to the two kinds of positions: boredom at forks, confusion at near-deterministic tokens, which explains the 94.0 % vs 86.7 % finished-answer accuracy at T 0.6 vs T 1.0 and the plain base's quartile pattern.
